title: Dependency and supply-chain security
subtitle: Most of the code you ship was written by strangers. Here is how to know what you run, and to trust it.

c.v: In March 2024, a developer named Andres Freund noticed something small. SSH logins on his Debian unstable (sid) systems used a lot of CPU. A tool called valgrind also showed odd errors.
He measured it. A failed login took about 0.8 seconds instead of 0.3. He traced the delay to liblzma, part of the xz compression tools. Then he found a backdoor.

The bad code was in xz versions 5.6.0 and 5.6.1. The part that started it was not in the Git repository that people read. It was only in the release tarballs, the files that Linux distributions download and build.
There, a line in one build file ran a hidden script at the end of
configure
. That script pulled more code out of two "test" files in the repository and put it into the library.
OpenSSH does not use liblzma directly. But Debian and several other distributions patch it to talk to systemd, and libsystemd depends on liblzma. That chain loaded the backdoor into the SSH server.
Freund pointed to weeks of activity by the person who committed the changes. He wrote that they were "either directly involved" or their system was badly compromised.
Luckily, few distributions had shipped 5.6.0 or 5.6.1 yet, and mostly in pre-release versions.
Look at what the attacker needed. Not a bug in your code. Just one trusted committer, one build step nobody read, and a dependency of a dependency.
Your app is mostly code that you did not write. Every library, every build tool and every
CI
action runs with your app's power. OWASP now ranks "Software Supply Chain Failures" third in its Top 10.
You met it in the
OWASP lesson
You face two separate problems:
Known flaws.
A library you use has a published bug, a
CVE
. You need to know you use it, and then upgrade.
Malicious code.
Someone put harmful code into a package, a build or a tool on purpose. No scanner knows about it yet.
The defenses answer three questions.
What exactly do we run?
A
lockfile
and an
SBOM
answer that.
Is any of it known to be bad?
A scanner answers that.
Did it really come from where we think?
Signatures and
provenance
answer that.
The key idea.

Treat every dependency, build tool and CI action as code that runs with your permissions. Fix the exact versions, know the full list, check where each piece came from, and give your pipeline the smallest power it needs.
Where attacks get in
Step through the path from source code to your app. Use Next and Back, or the ← and → keys.
Here are the common ways in:
Transitive dependencies
You add 5 packages. They can bring in hundreds more. OWASP says to track "not just your direct dependencies, but their (transitive) dependencies".
xz reached SSH through two hops.
Typosquatting
An attacker publishes
reqeusts
and waits for someone to mistype
requests
Dependency confusion
Your private package name also exists on a public index. From 25 to 30 December 2022, PyTorch nightly installs on Linux used a package called
torchtriton
from PyTorch's own index. Someone uploaded
torchtriton
to PyPI. Because the PyPI index took precedence, pip installed the fake one.
When imported, it read files such as
$HOME/.ssh/*
and sent them out through
DNS
queries.
Maintainer takeover.

An attacker gets a maintainer's account or token, or becomes a maintainer, as in xz. The Shai-Hulud worm of 2025 stole npm tokens and used them to publish bad versions of other packages. It reached over 500 package versions.
Compromised build systems and CI.
In March 2025, attackers moved several version tags of the GitHub Action
tj-actions/changed-files

to a malicious commit. The code read secrets from the runner's memory and printed them, encoded, in workflow logs. The bad code was live on 14 and 15 March 2025. GitHub's advisory says over 23,000 repositories used the action.
Lockfiles: know exactly what you install
A version range like
means "any 4.x from 4.17 up". Each install can pick a different version. A lockfile fixes the whole tree. npm's
package-lock.json
lets later installs "generate identical trees, regardless of intermediate dependency updates".
For each package it stores where it came from and an
integrity
hash.
So a swapped file fails the install.
In CI, use the strict install.
npm ci
needs a lockfile. If the lockfile and
package.json
disagree, it "will exit with an error, instead of updating the package lock". It never writes to either file.
Python, Go and Rust tools have the same idea under other names.
Commit the lockfile. Review changes to it like code: a new package in the lockfile is new code in production.
Scanning: when to upgrade
A scanner such as Dependabot compares your dependency graph with an advisory database. It alerts when a new advisory affects a version you use.
GitHub is clear about the limits: "Alerts can't catch every security issue", and new flaws can take time to reach the database.
A scanner finds known flaws. It does not find a fresh backdoor.
So when should you upgrade? OWASP says to choose versions on purpose and "upgrade only when there is need". It also says to watch for libraries that are no longer maintained.
OWASP gives no time frames. Here is our own suggestion:
Critical flaw in code you actually call:
upgrade within days, like any production bug.
Other alerts:
batch them into a regular update, for example every two weeks.
A brand-new release with no security reason:
wait, for example a few days. Others then have time to spot a bad release before you install it.
OWASP also suggests
staged rollouts
for updates, so one bad vendor release does not reach every system at once.
SBOM: the full list
A software bill of materials lists every component and version in what you ship. OWASP says to generate and manage it centrally for all your software.
When the next Log4Shell appears, you search your SBOMs instead of asking every team. Generate one per
build artifact
, in CI, and store it next to the artifact.
Signed builds and provenance
A lockfile says
which
version. It cannot say that the package was built from the source you think. The xz tarballs were not the same as git.
Provenance
is a record of how an artifact was built: the source, the build platform and the inputs.
SLSA
is a framework that grades this in build levels.
Build L0:
nothing. "L0 represents the lack of SLSA."
Build L1:
provenance exists. It helps prevent mistakes but "is trivial to bypass or forge".
Build L2:
a hosted build platform makes and signs the provenance. This stops tampering after the build.
Build L3:
a hardened build platform. Runs cannot affect each other, and build steps cannot reach the signing secret. This stops tampering during the build.
Signing used to mean guarding a long-lived private key.
Sigstore
removes that. The signer proves its identity with an
OIDC
token. Sigstore's
certificate authority
, Fulcio, issues a short-lived certificate, and the private key is thrown away after one signing.
Each signature goes into Rekor, a
transparency log
. It is
append-only
, and anyone can audit it.
You can use this today. On npm,
npm publish --provenance
from GitHub Actions or GitLab CI/CD signs provenance through Sigstore. Users check it with
npm audit signatures
npm is careful here: provenance "does not guarantee the package has no malicious code".
It proves where a package came from, not that the source is safe.
Hardening CI
Your CI runs third-party code with your secrets. The
CI/CD lesson
showed pinning briefly. Here is the full set.

blocks.v:
permissions:
  contents: read        # default for every job: read-only
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      # pin to a full commit SHA, with the version as a comment
      - uses: actions/checkout@<full-commit-sha>  # v4
      - run: npm ci

c.v: Pin actions to a full commit SHA.
GitHub warns that "a tag can be moved or deleted" by someone who gets access to the action's repo.
That is what happened to tj-actions.
Check that the SHA comes from the action's own repo, not a fork.
Give the token
least privilege
Start with read-only contents. Raise permissions only for the job that needs them.
Use short-lived OIDC credentials for deploys, as in
Secrets and key management
Be careful with
pull_request_target
It runs with privileges. Combined with checking out untrusted
pull request
code, GitHub says it can lead to repository takeover.
Keep pinned actions up to date.
Dependabot can update action references. Its alerts do not cover actions pinned to a SHA, so plan regular updates.
Build once and promote.
OWASP lists separation of duties, signed builds, environment-scoped secrets and promoting artifacts rather than rebuilding.
If a CI dependency is compromised, treat every secret it could read as leaked. Rotate them.
Lockfile plus
npm ci
Silent version changes and swapped files.
A bad version you chose to lock.
Low. Review lockfile diffs.
Vulnerability scanning
Known CVEs in versions you use.
New backdoors and flaws not yet in the database.
Low to start. Ongoing upgrade work.
SBOM per build
Slow answers to "are we affected?"
It only lists. It blocks nothing.
Low. One CI step.
Provenance and signatures
Packages not built from the claimed source and workflow.
Malicious code in the real source.
Medium. Build setup, and verify on install.
Actions pinned to SHA
Moved tags.
A bad commit you pinned yourself.
Medium. You must update pins.
Least-privilege CI token
Damage after a CI compromise.
The compromise itself.
Low.
Simple rule:
lock and scan everything from day one. Pin CI actions and cut token permissions next. Add provenance for anything you publish.

sections.name: At work
sections.title: At work: how a senior uses this

c.v: In review, treat a lockfile
diff
as a code diff. Ask:
"Why do we need this new package, and who maintains it?"
Before adding a dependency, check its downloads, maintainers, last release and its own dependency count. Prefer the standard library for small tasks.
Ask:
"If this package turned bad tonight, which secrets could it read?"
Install scripts and CI steps run with real credentials.
Use scoped or namespaced names for internal packages, and own the same names on public indexes. Point installs at one index you control.
Keep an SBOM per release, so "are we affected?" takes minutes.
Set a written patch deadline for critical CVEs, and track it like a bug.
Pin every third-party action to a SHA. Set
permissions: contents: read
at the top of every workflow.
Coding agents

add packages to fix problems. They can also suggest package names that do not exist. One study of 576,000 code samples found that, on average, at least 5.2% of the packages from commercial models did not exist. For open-source models it was 21.7%.
Attackers can register those names. This is called
slopsquatting
"List every direct dependency in this repo with its version, last release date and number of maintainers. Flag any package that is unmaintained or has fewer than 1,000 weekly downloads."
"Find every GitHub Action in .github/workflows that is not pinned to a full commit SHA. Propose the pinned line with the version as a comment. Do not change behaviour."
"Add a top-level
permissions: contents: read
to each workflow. Then list which jobs need more, and why."
Every package the agent added really exists, is the one you meant, and is in the lockfile.
The agent did not change the lockfile in ways the task did not need.
Each pinned SHA comes from the action's own repo, not a fork.
The agent did not add
pull_request_target
or wider token permissions to make a workflow pass.
No new install script runs during the build without a reason.
OWASP Top 10 and secure coding
: where supply-chain failures sit among the common flaws.
Secrets and key management
: what to rotate after a CI compromise.
CI/CD and trunk-based development
: build once, then promote.

q.v: In the 2024 xz backdoor, where was the line that started the hidden build step?

options.v: In a normal source file that reviewers read in Git.
In the release tarballs only. The Git repository did not have the line that started it.

why.v: Freund found that the line in build-to-host.m4 that ran the hidden script was only in the distributed tarballs, not in git.

q.v: . What is the main supply-chain risk?

options.v: Someone with access to that repo can move the v3 tag to a new, harmful commit.
Version 3 might have a CVE that Dependabot cannot report.

why.v: GitHub warns that a tag can be moved or deleted. In the tj-actions attack, tags were moved to a malicious commit. A full commit SHA cannot be moved.

q.v: Your app installs an internal package
from a private index, with the public index as an extra source. What best stops dependency confusion?

options.v: Give the internal package a very high version number.
Run a vulnerability scanner every night.
Own the name on the public index too, and install internal packages only from the index you control.

why.v: PyTorch was hit because pip preferred the public index. Its fix included a placeholder package on PyPI. A scanner only knows about published flaws.

q.v: A package's provenance is made by a script on a developer laptop and is not signed. What is the highest SLSA build level it can claim?

options.v: Build L1. Provenance exists, but it is easy to forge.
Build L2. Any provenance is enough.
Build L3. The build is hardened.

why.v: L2 needs a hosted build platform that signs the provenance. Unsigned provenance from a laptop shows how it was built, but anyone could fake it.

q.v: npm shows a verified provenance attestation for a package. What does that tell you?

options.v: The package contains no malicious code.
Which source repository and CI build produced it.
The package has no known CVEs.

why.v: Provenance links the package to its source and build. npm says it does not guarantee the package has no malicious code.
